exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Situations Where a Normal Approximation is Appropriate

question.text:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

  1. The probability that an inbox with $100$ emails contains $45$ spam emails, given that the probability that a single email is spam is $0.47.$
  2. The probability that less than $2$ light bulbs are defective from a box containing $20$ lightbulbs if the probability of a single bulb being defective is $0.12.$
  3. The probability of finding more than $16$ people with blood type A$-$ in a randomly selected sample of $50$ people, given that the probability that a randomly selected person has blood type A$-$ is $0.08.$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.47.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 100\cdot 0.47\\[5pt] &= 47 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 100\cdot (1-0.47) \\[5pt] &=53 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation II, we have $n=20$ and $p=0.12.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 20\cdot 0.12\\[5pt] &=2.4\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation III, we have $n=50$ and $p=0.08.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 50\cdot 0.08\\[5pt] &= 4\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

question.text:
Given that the random variable $X\sim B(110,0.5),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=65).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.00 \,$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$
$\, 1.8 \,$ $\, 0.9641 \,$ $\, 0.9649 \,$ $\, 0.9656 \,$
$\, 1.9 \,$ $\, 0.9713 \,$ $\, 0.9719 \,$ $\, 0.9726 \,$
$\, 2.0 \,$ $\, 0.9773 \,$ $\, 0.9778 \,$ $\, 0.9783 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=110$ and $p = 0.5.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 110\cdot 0.5\\[5pt] &= 55 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 110\cdot (1-0.5) \\[5pt] &=55 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (110)(0.5) = 55 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (110)(0.5)(1-0.5) = 27.5. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(55, 27.5).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X = 65).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X = 65) \approx P(64.5 \leq Y \leq 65.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(64.5 \leq Y \leq 65.5) &= P \left( \dfrac{64.5-55}{\sqrt{27.5}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{65.5-55}{\sqrt{27.5}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( 1.81 \leq Z \leq 2.00 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq 2.00) - P(Z < 1.81) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq 2.00) - P(Z \leq 1.81) \\[5pt] &= \Phi(2.00) - \Phi(1.81) \\[5pt] &=0.9773 - 0.9649\\[5pt] &=0.012 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(X = 65)\approx 0.012. \]

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0124.$

Here, we have $n=210$ and $p = 0.6.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 210\cdot 0.6\\[5pt] &= 126 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 210\cdot (1-0.6) \\[5pt] &=84 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (210)(0.6) = 126 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (210)(0.6)(1-0.6) = 50.4. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(126, 50.4).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(120 < X \leq 140).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(120 < X \leq 140) = P(121 \leq X \leq 140) \approx P(120.5 \leq Y \leq 140.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(120.5 \leq Y \leq 140.5) &= P\left(\dfrac{120.5-126}{\sqrt{50.4}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{140.5-126}{\sqrt{50.4}}\right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( -0.77 \leq Z \leq 2.04 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z\leq 2.04) - P(Z < -0.77) \\[5pt] &= P(Z\leq 2.04) - P(Z \leq -0.77) \\[5pt] &=\Phi(2.04)-\Phi(-0.77) \\[5pt] &=0.9793-0.2206 \\[5pt] &=0.7587 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(120 < X \leq 140) \approx 0.759. \] Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.7602.$
